subject: EN
title: Reading Part 3: The business of voluntourism
source: MSA Berlin 2024 Englisch, Reading Part 3; adapted from The Guardian, 13 Sept 2018
body:
(1) Every year, millions of people from wealthy nations travel to poor countries, hoping to do good. University students want to spend a school break or part of a summer giving back, perhaps even to improve their CV. Christians go with their churches for one- or two-week missions. All seek personal growth, connection to those less fortunate, and the satisfaction of making a difference. But the booming business of "voluntourism" supports practices and institutions that actually do harm.

(2) Voluntourism is an outgrowth of the ecotourism movement of the 1990s. According to Pippa Biddle, author of a forthcoming book on voluntourism, travellers rebelled against package trips and resorts and wanted a more authentic experience – and they were willing to pay for it. Many charities in developing countries run such programmes and collect fees from volunteers. "It used to be if you wanted to volunteer abroad, you wrote letters to overseas contacts," says Claire Bennett, co-author of Learning Service. "Now you can buy a volunteer experience with a few clicks."

(3) Voluntourism may be driven by noble feelings, but it is built on perverse economics. Many organisations offer volunteers the chance to dig wells, build schools and do other construction projects in poor villages. It's easy to understand why it's done this way: if a charity hired locals for its unskilled work, it would be spending money. If it uses volunteers who pay to be there, it's raising money.

(4) But the last thing a Guatemalan highland village needs is imported unskilled labour. People are desperate for jobs. Public works serve the community better and last longer when locals do them. Besides, long-term change happens when people can solve their own problems, rather than having things done for them.

(5) "There are few things more cringeworthy than watching 20 British schoolgirls trying to build a well under the scalding Nepalese heat," one Durham University student wrote about her trip to an orphanage. Villagers, afraid of offending their visitors, say nothing. An American volunteer in Tanzania recalled: "We were so bad at the most basic construction work that each night the men had to take down the structurally unsound bricks we had laid and rebuild the structure so that, when we woke up in the morning, we would be unaware of our failure."

(6) Defenders of voluntourism claim that its real value is to change the visitor. But while it's definitely more transformational for the visitor than the host, it's not clear how significant the effects are. A study of 162 Americans who travelled to Honduras to build houses after Hurricane Mitch in 1998 found that years later, this work hadn't made better people out of the volunteers. And even if the houses they built didn't fall over, they were expensive. The houses in Honduras built by international volunteers cost $30,000 apiece, including airfare, while local organisations could build them for $2,000. If well-wishers had given money instead of labour, 15 times more houses could have been built. The helpful choice would have been to stay at home. Money goes far in poor countries. Two thousand dollars can pay for a week-long trip taken by an unskilled American volunteer – or it could pay the salary of a village teacher for four months.

(7) Lourdes Milian, who manages Hope of Life, one of the biggest volunteer organisations near Guatemala City, said that during summer and school vacations, about 400 volunteers come every week, and, on average, 150 during other weeks. Volunteers, then, bring at least $9m a year to Hope of Life. Hope of Life had a budget of $15.7m in 2016, which funds its many programmes: projects in villages to dig wells and build schools, baby rescue, the feeding centre, the hospital. But when I visited, it seemed clear that not much money was being spent on its weakest, disabled residents, while a lot of investment has gone towards making the volunteer experience as comfortable as possible – and as emotionally rewarding.

(8) McGehee at Virginia Tech would like to see voluntourism recast as "transformational tourism", with visitors rewarded by getting a better understanding of people's lives, and the way the economics of charity work. By all means, visit people who need help, she says. But do it beside them and hear who they are, she adds. Get to know them and not all those stereotypes about them. And then go home and see if there's something you're doing that somehow contributes to their problems.

subject: EN
title: Reading Part 1: What to do in and around Quebec (Canada)
source: MSA Berlin 2024 Englisch, Reading Part 1, Texte leicht gekürzt
body:
**The people**

- **Frank**: Strolling through the winter landscape with kids and grandparents? Definitely not for Frank. Touring Canada alone, he wants to be around other athletes to test his limits and explore the wild around the city. And then he will post pictures of his experiences in his fashion and travel blog. Maybe he should therefore also choose a tour that polishes up his knowledge on how to take nicer pictures.
- **Ronida** is in Quebec with her two teens. They are into all sorts of entertainment. Since she wants to know more about the history of the city, this only works if there is some sort of playful approach. But they need to be back at the hotel for dinner. And they all love recreational activities in nature. As long as the kids have their hot beverage, they are out in the woods and this trip is not too tough, they are up for it.
- **Hei-Lin** is into nature and photography. That's why she is looking for a tour that shows her the beautiful Canadian landscape and offers chances for taking great pictures. She is not exactly a sportswoman, so this tour should not be too challenging. After a tour in the woods, she would like to taste the flavors of Quebec City, preferably in a high-class environment.
- **Agatha** is interested in a walking tour that combines historical facts with thrilling entertainment. It shouldn't take too long though. Apart from that, she has the feeling that the way people dress tells you more about a place than anything else. A tour with an expert in this field could teach her a lot, and maybe she could also get some input for her own wardrobe.
- **Jonathan** would like to spend a tasteful evening in downtown Quebec. New people in a nice atmosphere and a few drinks to round off the night are exactly what he likes about travelling. Certainly, this is hardly possible without the proper outfit. Someone who could advise him what to wear that night would be pretty useful.

**The tours**

- **A) Historical and food tour**: Quebec City is known for food and history, and this evening tour gives you both. Visit top restaurants and historical sights. We will visit five different gourmet stops, each providing one course of your dinner, while your guide elaborates on points of interest inside Old Quebec. Not wheelchair accessible; since alcoholic drinks are served, the minimum age is 18.
- **B) Crime walking tour**: Discover the darkest years of New France on an animated 90-minute crime walking evening tour in Old Quebec. Follow ghostly guides to learn about terrible crimes, arrests and executions that happened centuries ago. Walk the streets after dark and discover the secrets of this historic and haunted neighborhood. Children are allowed with their parents.
- **C) Ski-shoeing tour**: Discover the winter beauty of Jacques-Cartier National Park on this roughly five-hour ski-shoeing hike, a mix of cross-country skiing and snowshoeing that provides intense exercise amid peaceful forest landscapes. Warm up with hot chocolate, stop for lunch, and keep watch for wildlife. This small-group tour is limited to eight people who are not afraid of a true physical challenge.
- **D) Virtual reality tour**: First, a 40-minute 3D movie: live history as if you were there and dive into the moments that made Quebec City world-famous. Then an interactive phase with an electronic tablet: test your knowledge and learn more about the city's past in a fun and entertaining way for the whole family.
- **E) Fashion and stylist tour**: Discover the local shopping scene and its fashion DNA with a professional stylist. Learn the art of styling your body features as your stylist pulls pieces for you to explore and try. A mini style consultation followed by recommendations and a hands-on shopping tour where you can ask any fashion and style-related questions.
- **F) Electric fat bike winter tour**: Hop on your bike and follow your guide along quiet trails, experiencing winter beauty, with plenty of opportunities to stop for photos. Wildlife can be easier to spot in the winter landscape. Stop at a heated tipi tent for lunch and a hot drink. Regardless of your fitness level, the electric motor makes it easy to traverse the snowy park. Afterwards you are returned by minivan to your hotel.
- **G) Blue hour photo tour**: A two-hour tour in the tourist part of the city, starting just before sunset. A professional photographer advises you on your photography skills and helps you improve in order to make you a better photographer, especially when natural light becomes darker, while discovering the beautiful places of Quebec City.
